subject: physics
title: The Hertzsprung-Russell Diagram
welcome_lead: Plot luminosity against temperature and watch stars sort themselves into clear groups.
meta_desc: A-Level Astrophysics adventure on the HR diagram and stellar evolution stages.
final_note: Main sequence is where stars spend most of their lives fusing hydrogen.

concepts.def: Plot of luminosity vs surface temperature.
Cool, large, very luminous evolved star.
Reversed: hot on left, cool on right.

walkthroughs.body_html: x-axis: temperature decreasing left to right (or spectral class O B A F G K M). y-axis: luminosity in solar units, log scale. Most stars lie on the main sequence.
Sun moves: main sequence → red giant (off MS up-right) → planetary nebula → white dwarf (lower-left). Massive stars instead become supergiants then supernovae.
Upper right: cool but very luminous, hence huge — red giants/supergiants. Lower left: hot but dim, therefore tiny — white dwarfs. Diagonal band: main sequence.

mcqs.q: On an HR diagram, the main sequence is a:
options: Horizontal line
Vertical line
Diagonal band top-left to bottom-right
Single point

mcqs.q: White dwarfs sit on the HR diagram:
options: Top right
Top left
Bottom right
Bottom left

mcqs.q: Why do more massive stars have shorter main-sequence lifetimes than smaller ones?
options: Yes — but only after billions of years on Earth's scale.
All stars live the same time on the main sequence regardless of mass.
More massive stars live longer because they have more fuel.
They burn through their hydrogen fuel much faster because higher core temperature drives nuclear fusion at a vastly greater rate.

mcqs.q: Why do brighter-looking stars not necessarily have higher luminosity?
options: Apparent brightness depends on both luminosity and distance — a closer dim star can look brighter than a distant luminous one.
Apparent brightness depends only on the star's temperature.
Brighter-looking stars are always intrinsically more luminous.
More massive stars live longer because they have more fuel.

mcqs.q: Do all stars end their lives as supernovae?
options: No — only sufficiently massive stars (above about 8 solar masses) explode as supernovae; lower-mass stars become white dwarfs.
More massive stars live longer because they have more fuel.
Yes — every star eventually explodes.
Yes — but only after billions of years on Earth's scale.
